item.title: Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
item.description:
Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the worldByROD MCGUIRK Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 1:18 AM
MELBOURNE, Australia -- An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack thanked well-wishers around the world Monday and revealed she had been discharged from a hospital where she spent the past month.
In her first public statement since being struck by a SUV on Oct. 19, Helen Haines said she was “very pleased to confirm” she had left Melbourne’s The Alfred hospital.
Witnesses said she was repeatedly rammed by the vehicle outside her electorate office.
The 65-year-old independent lawmaker said she would remain in Melbourne for the “rehabilitation stage” of her recovery. Her staff would not disclose where her rehabilitation would take place for privacy reasons.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across (my electorate) Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing,” she added.
Haines was in critical condition hours after she was struck when she was flown to Melbourne by helicopter from her hometown of Wangaratta, 236 kilometers (147 miles) to the northeast.
Surgeons amputated both her legs within a few days.
The hospital listed her as critical until Oct. 24 when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable. She had been listed as stable since Nov. 6.

item.title: Pope bids 'hasta luego' to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip
item.description:
Pope bids 'hasta luego' to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip
Pope Leo XIV has bid farewell to his beloved homeland of PeruByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press, ASTRID SUÁREZ Associated Press, and LUIS ANDRES HENAO Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 9:43 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
LIMA, Peru -- LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.
During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo's final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended.
The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public.
For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.
“It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” Leo said at the end of Mass.
Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.

item.title: Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
item.description:
Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
Japan said it has protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian warplanes temporarily entered Japanese airspace off the country’s southwestern coast on Tuesday as tensions escalate between the two sidesByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 1:18 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TOKYO -- Japan said it strongly protested to Moscow on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace off its southwestern coast, the latest incident fueling escalating tensions between the neighbors.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters the suspected Russian aircraft early Tuesday violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes near Fukuoka, long enough for the Air Self-Defense Force to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
Japan's government has lodged "an extremely stern protest" and “strongly” demanded preventive measures be taken, Koizumi said. He did not specify the types of aircraft involved.
“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said. “It is absolutely unacceptable.”
The Russian aircraft flew across the Tsushima Strait, then headed south and flew above the waters between Taiwan and Japan's westernmost island of Yonaguni, Koizumi said.
Separately, South Korea’s military said several Russian military aircraft temporarily entered the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan on Monday, though they did not violate South Korean airspace.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the military had detected the aircraft before they entered the zone and scrambled fighter jets. The South’s military did not disclose the number of Russian aircraft it detected or what types of planes they were.
Koizumi did not comment on why the violations took place but said Japan co...

item.title: A fire in a building in southern Thailand kills 11 people
item.description:
A fire in a building in southern Thailand kills 11 people
A fire has burned through a building in southern Thailand and killed 11 peopleByThe Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 12:46 AM
BANGKOK -- A fire burned through a building in southern Thailand early Monday, killing 11 people, authorities said.
The fire started around 2 a.m. in the building in Phuket that has a motorcycle rental shop on the ground floor and residences on the upper floors, officials of the local government said. It took firefighters about an hour to bring the fire under control.
There were 17 other people who were slightly injured.
Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but initial investigations found an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started.

item.title: Macron leaves summit of French-speaking nations with leadership dispute on hold
item.description:
Macron leaves summit of French-speaking nations with leadership dispute on hold
French President Emmanuel Macron left a summit of French-speaking nations on Monday with uncertainty still hanging over the organization’s leadership after a dispute between Rwanda and CongoByLORIAN BELANGER Associated Press, SOPHENG CHEANG Associated Press, and GRANT PECK Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 5:10 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
SIEM REAP, Cambodia -- French President Emmanuel Macron left a summit of French-speaking nations on Monday with uncertainty still hanging over the organization's leadership after a dispute between Rwanda and Congo roiled the proceedings.
After days of intense negotiations in the capital of Cambodia, member states decided that the incumbent secretary-general, Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo, will stay for another year before making way for a new leader of the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
Mushikiwabo was seeking a third term at the summit, which Congo had opposed, going as far as threatening to leave the OIF if she was reelected.
Congo has more than 110 million people — far exceeding France’s population of 70 million — and its withdrawal would be a significant blow to the organization.
Congo, the United States and U.N. experts accuse Rwanda of backing the M23, one of about 100 armed groups vying for a foothold in mineral-rich eastern Congo, along the border with Rwanda. Rwanda’s government consistently denies backing armed groups in Congo.
The French president’s office welcomed the one-year postponement and said it would allow the organization "to overcome divisions and preserve the consensus in the francophone family.”
Congo’s Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner said on X that “a wise compromise” would preserve unity in the Francophonie.
Macron held bilateral talks, including with Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet and Vietnamese leader To Lam, and attended the summit of the loose confederation of 90 member st...

item.title: Army airstrike kills at least 13 in West Kordofan, says rights group
item.description:
Army airstrike kills at least 13 in West Kordofan, says rights group
A rights group says an army airstrike killed at least 13 peopleByThe Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 12:50 PM
CAIRO -- A Sudanese army airstrike killed at least 13 people and destroyed several homes in western Sudan in a country ravaged by more than three years of fighting between the army and its rival paramilitary, a local rights group said Monday.
Women and children were among those killed in the strike in the Abu Qalb area of Abu Zabad locality in West Kordofan, according to the Emergency Lawyers, a group that tracks violence throughout the war in Sudan. The AP couldn’t independently verify the toll.
The war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises since it broke out in April 2023, killing at least 59,000 people, displacing around 13 million and pushing parts of the country into famine, according to aid organizations.
The Emergency Lawyers blamed the army for the airstrike in West Kordofan.

item.title: Paraguay’s ousted president moved to military prison after reports of gym and suite in custody
item.description:
Paraguay’s ousted president moved to military prison after reports of gym and suite in custody
Former Paraguayan President Santiago Peña is being moved to a military prison as he awaits trial over the collapse of Ueno BankByISABEL DEBRE Associated Press, NAYARA BASTCHKE Associated Press, and JORGE SAENZ Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 1:59 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay -- A Paraguayan judge on Monday ordered former President Santiago Peña moved to a military prison after reports that he had been held in a suite with a private gym, as he awaits trial over the implosion of a major digital lender, which toppled his government earlier this month.
Judge Osmar Legal ordered Peña transferred from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital, Asunción, where local media reported that his quarters also included a private bathroom and a spacious dining room.
Under the court order, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, Peña will now be held at the Viñas Cué military prison, apart from other detainees.
President Pedro Alliana opened a news conference Monday by announcing that he had ordered the dismissal of the regiment’s commander, Col. José David Daiub, following allegations that Peña had received special treatment there.
Alliana, who served as Peña’s vice president, pledged to give prosecutors whatever resources they need to investigate the bank’s collapse.
“Paraguayans deserve to know the truth,” he said.
Peña is in pretrial detention on charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Prosecutors allege that he used his influence to steer public money to Ueno Bank, a lender used by more than half Paraguay’s adults, as its executives made large insider loans to companies linked to the bank’s owners. He denies wrongdoing.

item.title: EU accuses Russia of stalling Ukraine peace talks to target power plants as winter nears
item.description:
EU accuses Russia of stalling Ukraine peace talks to target power plants as winter nears
The bloc imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks, financial institutions.ByLORNE COOK Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 5:20 AM
BRUSSELS -- European Union countries on Monday accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the war in Ukraine while it bombs power plants and other infrastructure to make life even harder for civilians as winter closes in.
The bloc also imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, and targeted several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil and petroleum products. It slapped asset freezes and travel bans on dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation.
At talks in Brussels, EU foreign ministers said the priority in Ukraine should be to secure a ceasefire and then a real peace agreement. They said that Russia started the nearly five-year war and must now be the one to make concessions, and they rejected any fresh demands.
"We actually don’t have a ceasefire and they continue to weaken Ukraine and kill people every single day,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters after chairing the meeting.
After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.
But the Europeans have likened it to the “treaty” that Russia offered NATO before launching its full-scale war in 2022. They see it as an attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to how they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.

item.title: Cape Verde’s president is reelected for a second 5-year term, provisional results show
item.description:
Cape Verde’s president is reelected for a second 5-year term, provisional results show
Cape Verde’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second term, defeating five challengers, including the country’s first female presidential candidateByThe Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 2:38 AM
PRAIA, Cape Verde -- PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Cape Verde ’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second five-year term, beating five challengers, including the first woman presidential candidate in the country’s history, provisional results show.
Neves called his reelection as president of the Atlantic island nation off West Africa “a great victory.” The election was dominated by high unemployment and the high cost of living, which has fueled emigration.
Provisional results showed Neves comfortably edged out his opponents, garnering 64% of the vote while Joana Rosa, the main opposition candidate, won 31.4%.
Rosa called Neves to concede defeat.
The small country has a history of smooth transfers of power and is one of the most stable in a region fraught with tense elections.

Turnout was low, with only 31.7% of the 418,000 registered voters casting a ballot.
Neves said the low turnout could be explained by high emigration, population movements within the country and outdated voter records. He promised a study to examine the issue.

item.title: Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
item.description:
Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
Prince William and Princess Catherine have arrived in India for a three-day visitByRAFIQ MAQBOOL Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 11:45 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MUMBAI, India -- MUMBAI, India (AP) — Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since she was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.
The U.K. royal couple began their visit in Mumbai and will attend the Earthshot Prize awards ceremony on Tuesday. Founded by William, the annual environmental prize awards five winners $1.3 million each to expand solutions addressing climate change.
The ceremony, expected to be the biggest since the prize was established in 2020, will feature several prominent guests including Indian cricket great Sachin Tendulkar, actors Alia Bhatt and Rami Malek and British pop group Take That, which will make its debut performance in India.
“India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country,” William posted on social media.
Shortly after their arrival, the royal couple took part in a game of street cricket in an alley in Ballard Estate, a neighborhood in Mumbai. Street cricket, a common sight across the city, is an integral part of everyday life in Mumbai.
